title: Why You Should Never Punish Your Entire Class For The Behavior Of A Few ass-for-the-behavior-of-a-few/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Prompted by a friend's story of a child kept in from recess for classmates' misbehavior, Linsin argues against the common practice of collectively punishing an entire class for the actions of a few, even though it reliably produces short-term compliance. The core problem, he explains, is that it alienates well-behaved students, who have an acute sense of fairness and will notice — and resent — being punished for something they didn't do. He distinguishes this from redoing or reteaching a routine, which he does recommend, but only when the routine itself, not isolated misbehavior, was performed poorly by essentially the whole class. Critically, redoing a routine takes nothing away from students; it simply reinforces that instructions were meant seriously. His guidance is to hold individual students accountable individually through the classroom management plan, reserving class-wide reteaching only for genuinely class-wide performance problems.
points: Collectively punishing an entire class for a few students' misbehavior reliably produces short-term compliance but breeds long-term resentment.
Well-behaved students have an acute sense of fairness and will notice and resent being punished for others' actions.
Redoing or reteaching a routine is appropriate only when the routine itself, not isolated misbehavior, was performed poorly by nearly everyone.
Redoing a routine takes nothing away from students — it reinforces that instructions were meant to be followed precisely.
Individual misbehavior should always be addressed individually through the classroom management plan, not through class-wide punishment.
quotes: The problem with the strategy, however, is that it alienates your most well-behaved students.
Students from kindergarten on up have an acute sense of fairness. Although they may not always voice their frustration to you, you can bet they’ll bring it up at the dinner table.
First, you should never redo a routine if the problem is just a few students.
Also, when you redo a routine, it’s not because of misbehavior. It’s because your class did the routine incorrectly.
Finally, when you ask students to repeat a routine, you’re not taking anything away from them. They aren’t missing recess or arriving late to lunch or losing out on class points.

To sum up, when individual students misbehave, hold them accountable individually by following your classroom management plan . If it’s more than one or two at a time, then it’s a sign you must become a more vigilant observer.
